doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
title: The avant-garde and what it means to him
summary: Ware says the avant-garde was meant to be unstealable and he now thinks it is European.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, what about the avant garde. You touched on it a little bit with Archie Shepp and the people like Leroy Jones has written books and you span the entire spectrum in a sense, when they talk about you. For instance, Leroy Jones said you've been around. You're the prime innovator, but you've been around so long, people have had a chance to pick up. So when they talk about you, they talk about really the entire history of black music, black sophisticated music, on the level we're talking about. So how do you feel about avantgarde or making a record with say, with Archie Shepp, or with like (unintelligible) Beautiful Things, which is classified strictly avantgarde.

Well, personally, avantgarde, like they say, is outside, you know. For a while, I believed that they did that to keep what they said cats was stealing their music. It was that black-white thing again. So they said they going to play something that they won't be able to steal, which was a lie, and if you notice now, the avantgarde is actually Euro-
pean. You know, it's what -- it's what it's all about.

What I mean by it's all about. Back in the '60s, there was these guys. I remember they had a discussion on avantgarde versus jazz. That goes back to what they call Dixieland, with what would you say? Jazz? Dixieland or either swing versus bop, you know.
